## TL;DR

Fixed the remote host lock queue cleanup bug and an adjacent zero-wait gate hang found during validation. The queue scan now remembers that a live higher-priority waiter requires deferral while continuing through the directory to remove dead-PID entries. The test uses controlled process lifetimes, checks only its own queue entries, and has no wall-clock upper bound. The pool and host-config suites passed together with 197 tests.

## Work and rationale

The original test seeded a live high-priority queue entry and a dead high-priority entry, then ran `hostLockShell` with a two-second wait budget. It expected the shell to defer to the live waiter, clean the dead entry, time out, and never run the inner command. The test chose the dead PID by adding one million to the Vitest worker PID, compared the entire shared wait directory with exactly one expected entry, and imposed a wall-clock ceiling. Each assumption could fail for reasons unrelated to lock behavior.

I replaced the arithmetic PID with a child process that the test explicitly terminates. The test starts the lock shell with a short pre-scan delay, waits until its PID is known, then creates the terminated child's queue entry. This prevents the dead PID from being mistaken for the lock shell's own PID. It checks that the dead entry was removed and its own live priority blocker remains, without requiring unrelated waiters to be absent. The two-second lock wait remains unchanged; the subprocess test has a 30-second runner timeout and no elapsed-time ceiling.

During focused verification, the dead entry still remained. Tracing `hostLockShell` showed why: the queue loop set `_defer=1` when it found a live higher-priority waiter, then broke immediately. Since queue filenames are scanned in order, a live entry could sort ahead of a dead entry and prevent cleanup from reaching it. The production change removes the early break. The scan records that it must defer but continues removing dead PIDs before the shell sleeps and retries.

The first scoped remote check then exposed another timeout in the same host-lock suite. A zero-wait caller could loop forever when the `.acquire-gate` directory was already occupied: the gate retry only checked elapsed wait when `WAIT > 0`. I changed that check so a zero-wait caller exits after its first failed gate acquisition attempt, matching the outer acquisition loop. A new test pre-creates the gate and verifies the timeout exit without running the inner command.

I documented the queue scan ordering bug, the test fixture pitfalls, and the zero-wait gate edge in `docs/debugging-check-failures.md`.

## Approaches tried

I ran the regression test in isolation, then ran the whole pool test file concurrently with `remote-host-config.test.ts`. The initial PID-offset and child-process fixtures exposed the production early-break behavior. After fixing it, the concurrent suites passed. The first RepoOS scoped run had a separate timed-out real-process test in the lock suite, which led to inspection of the zero-wait gate retry path and the additional fix/test.

## Challenges and blockers

The first test changes alone were insufficient because the production scan genuinely skipped cleanup based on filename order. A subsequent scoped check surfaced the adjacent zero-wait gate loop. After both fixes, the full pool and host-config suites passed together: 197 tests. The final `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passed: the remote run passed all 154 selected test files (2,749 passed, one skipped), and the browser gate, local formatting, lint, build, safety checks, rendered contrast, and UI smoke passed.

## Key learnings

A queue scan that cleans stale entries and decides whether to defer must finish examining the queue even after it finds a reason to wait. Early exit can leave stale state based solely on filename order. Zero-wait semantics also need to cover lock acquisition sub-loops, not just the outer polling loop. For process-backed tests, control the process lifecycle, avoid exact assertions on shared directories, and separate the configured wait budget from scheduler-sensitive wall-clock timing.
